title: Νὺξ ἄϋπνος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Book 10 opens on a night without sleep in the Achaean camp. The other chiefs are asleep, but Agamemnon lies awake, groaning at the fires of the Trojans and the plight of his army, and decides to seek counsel from Nestor. Menelaus, too, is sleepless and afraid for the Argives, and goes to find his brother, who is already arming. Agamemnon says that Zeus has turned his favour to Hector, sends Menelaus to call Ajax and Idomeneus, and goes himself to Nestor. He finds the old man in bed with his arms beside him, and Nestor, raising himself from his bed, asks who walks the camp alone at night. Agamemnon names himself, tells how fear keeps him from sleep, and proposes that they go down together to the guards.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι μὲν παρὰ νηυσὶν ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν
εὗδον παννύχιοι μαλακῷ δεδμημένοι ὕπνῳ·
sentences.tr:
alloi men para nēusin aristēes Panachaiōn
heudon pannychioi malakōi dedmēmenoi hypnōi·
sentences.l:
Others, indeed, by the ships, the best men of the Achaeans all together,
were sleeping the whole night through, overcome by soft sleep;
sentences.i: The other best men of all the Achaeans were sleeping by the ships the whole night through, overcome by soft sleep;
sentences.n: This is the first line of Book 10. ἄλλοι μέν sets the sleeping chiefs against the one man awake, who comes in the next line. ἀριστῆες ‘the best men’ is built on ἄριστος ‘best’, and Παναχαιῶν ‘of the Achaeans all together’ is the genitive plural of Παναχαιοί, a name for the whole army. εὗδον is the imperfect of εὕδω ‘sleep’; παννύχιοι ‘all night long’ is an adjective agreeing with the sleepers, where English uses an adverb. δεδμημένοι is the perfect passive participle of δάμνημι (= δαμάζω) ‘overcome’, with ὕπνῳ ‘by sleep’ in the dative; μαλακῷ is ‘soft’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα ποιμένα λαῶν
ὕπνος ἔχε γλυκερὸς πολλὰ φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντα.
sentences.tr:
all’ ouk Atreïdēn Agamemnona poimena laōn
hypnos eche glykeros polla phresin hormainonta.
sentences.l:
but not Atreus’-son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
sleep held, sweet, as he pondered many things in his wits.
sentences.i: But sweet sleep did not hold Agamemnon, son of Atreus, shepherd of the people, as he pondered many things in his mind.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐκ turns from the sleepers to the one man awake. Ἀτρεΐδην is the object of ἔχε, an imperfect, ‘kept hold of’; the object comes first and the subject ὕπνος after it, with γλυκερός ‘sweet’ held back to the end of the clause: ‘sleep held him not, sweet sleep’. The participle ὁρμαίνοντα agrees with Ἀγαμέμνονα: ὁρμαίνω is ‘turn over in the mind, ponder’, and πολλά ‘many things’ is its object. φρεσίν is the epic dative plural of φρήν. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is a stock title of a leader, and the poet gives it to Nestor too at line 73.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀστράπτῃ πόσις Ἥρης ἠϋκόμοιο
τεύχων ἢ πολὺν ὄμβρον ἀθέσφατον ἠὲ χάλαζαν
ἢ νιφετόν, ὅτε πέρ τε χιὼν ἐπάλυνεν ἀρούρας,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an astraptēi posis Hērēs ēÿkomoio
teuchōn ē polyn ombron athesphaton ēe chalazan
ē nipheton, hote per te chiōn epalynen arouras,
sentences.l:
And as when the husband of Hera, fine-haired, flashes lightning,
making either much rain, immense, or hail,
or a snowfall, just when snow has powdered the plough-lands,
sentences.i: As when the husband of fine-haired Hera sends lightning, making either a heavy rain, an immense one, or hail, or a fall of snow, just when snow has powdered the plough-lands,
sentences.n: A simile begins, and its sentence runs on to line 10, so the unit stops at the comma after ἀρούρας. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀστράπτῃ is ‘and as when he flashes lightning’ (ὅτ’ ἂν is Attic ὅταν; the subjunctive makes it general). πόσις Ἥρης ‘the husband of Hera’ is Zeus, unnamed; ἠϋκόμοιο ‘fine-haired’ is the stock epithet, with the epic genitive -οιο (= Attic -ου). τεύχων ‘making’ governs the whole list of what he makes: ὄμβρον, χάλαζαν, νιφετόν, and in line 8 a mouth of war. ἀθέσφατον ‘immense’ goes with ὄμβρον. ἐπάλυνεν is the aorist of ἐπαλύνω, a rare verb, ‘powdered, sprinkled over’; the aorist after ὅτε πέρ τε states what snow does. ἀρούρας ‘plough-lands’.

sentences.t:
ἠέ ποθι πτολέμοιο μέγα στόμα πευκεδανοῖο,
ὣς πυκίν’ ἐν στήθεσσιν ἀνεστενάχιζ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
νειόθεν ἐκ κραδίης,
sentences.tr:
ēe pothi ptolemoio mega stoma peukedanoio,
hōs pykin’ en stēthessin anestenachiz’ Agamemnōn
neiothen ek kradiēs,
sentences.i: or somewhere the great mouth of sharp war, so Agamemnon heaved groan after groan in his chest, from the depths of his heart,
sentences.n: ἠέ ποθι ‘or somewhere’ continues the list begun in line 6, after τεύχων. πτολέμοιο is the epic form of πολέμου ‘of war’, with the genitive -οιο. στόμα ‘mouth’ is the opening of war, from which it pours out. πευκεδανοῖο is a word whose meaning is not known: ‘sharp’ is the usual guess, and the formation is not certain (it may be linked to πεύκη ‘pine’, as in the ἐχεπευκές of 1.51). ὣς … ἀνεστενάχιζ’ is the other half of the simile: ‘so Agamemnon groaned’. πυκίν’ (πυκινά) ‘thickly’ is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘in close succession’; the imperfect ἀνεστενάχιζε is a repeated action. νειόθεν ‘from the bottom’; κραδίης is the genitive of κραδίη, the epic form of καρδία ‘heart’.

sentences.t: τρομέοντο δέ οἱ φρένες ἐντός.
sentences.tr: tromeonto de hoi phrenes entos.
sentences.l: and his wits trembled within him.
sentences.i: and his wits trembled within him.
sentences.n: τρομέοντο is the uncontracted imperfect of τρομέω ‘tremble’ (Attic ἐτρόμουν; there is no augment). οἱ is a dative of the pronoun, ‘for him’, which English turns into ‘his’. φρένες ‘wits’ are the seat of thought and feeling in the chest; ἐντός ‘within’. The simile ends here: the sky’s threat of storm and Agamemnon’s trembling are set side by side.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὅτ’ ἐς πεδίον τὸ Τρωϊκὸν ἀθρήσειε,
θαύμαζεν πυρὰ πολλὰ τὰ καίετο Ἰλιόθι πρὸ
αὐλῶν συρίγγων τ’ ἐνοπὴν ὅμαδόν τ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr:
ētoi hot’ es pedion to Trōïkon athrēseie,
thaumazen pyra polla ta kaieto Iliothi pro
aulōn syringōn t’ enopēn homadon t’ anthrōpōn.
sentences.l:
Now whenever he looked out to the Trojan plain,
he marvelled at the many fires which were burning before Ilios,
at the sound of pipes and panpipes and the uproar of men.
sentences.i: Whenever he looked out over the Trojan plain, he marvelled at the many fires burning before Ilios, at the sound of pipes and panpipes and the uproar of men.
sentences.n: ἤτοι (printed as one word by the edition) opens the first of two clauses, answered by αὐτὰρ ὅτ’ in line 14. ἀθρήσειε is an optative of ἀθρέω ‘look at, gaze’; after ὅτε it marks repetition in the past, ‘whenever he looked’, and the imperfect θαύμαζεν ‘marvelled’ matches it. τὰ καίετο: the article is a relative, ‘which’, and πυρά, a neuter plural, takes a singular verb, καίετο ‘were burning’. Ἰλιόθι ‘at Ilios’ has the place suffix -θι, and πρό ‘before’ follows it. αὐλῶν and συρίγγων are genitives depending on ἐνοπήν ‘sound’: an αὐλός is a reed pipe, and a σῦριγξ is a pipe of reeds, usually understood as a panpipe. ἐνοπή is a voice or cry, here of instruments. ὅμαδόν ‘uproar’ is the noise of a crowd.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅτ’ ἐς νῆάς τε ἴδοι καὶ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν,
πολλὰς ἐκ κεφαλῆς προθελύμνους ἕλκετο χαίτας
ὑψόθ’ ἐόντι Διί, μέγα δ’ ἔστενε κυδάλιμον κῆρ.
sentences.tr:
autar hot’ es nēas te idoi kai laon Achaiōn,
pollas ek kephalēs prothelymnous helketo chaitas
hypsoth’ eonti Dii, mega d’ estene kydalimon kēr.
sentences.l:
But whenever he looked to the ships and the people of the Achaeans,
many from his head, root and all, he pulled out, locks,
to Zeus being on high, and greatly he groaned in his glorious heart.
sentences.i: But whenever he looked to the ships and the army of the Achaeans, he pulled out many locks from his head, root and all, to Zeus on high, and groaned greatly in his glorious heart.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅτ’ answers ἤτοι ὅτ’ of line 11: two sights, two reactions. ἴδοι is an optative of repetition, as ἀθρήσειε was. προθελύμνους ‘root and all’ (a word built on θέλυμνα ‘foundations’) agrees with χαίτας ‘locks of hair’; ἕλκετο is the middle, ‘pulled out for himself’. ὑψόθ’ ἐόντι Διί, ‘to Zeus who is on high’, is a dative of the person toward whom the gesture is made, whether as appeal or as reproach is not said. κυδάλιμον ‘glorious’ is a stock epithet, here of the heart; κῆρ ‘heart’ is an accusative of respect, ‘groaned in his heart’. ἔστενε is the imperfect of στένω ‘groan’.

sentences.t:
ἥδε δέ οἱ κατὰ θυμὸν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλὴ
Νέστορ’ ἔπι πρῶτον Νηλήϊον ἐλθέμεν ἀνδρῶν,
εἴ τινά οἱ σὺν μῆτιν ἀμύμονα τεκτήναιτο,
ἥ τις ἀλεξίκακος πᾶσιν Δαναοῖσι γένοιτο.
sentences.tr:
hēde de hoi kata thymon aristē phaineto boulē
Nestor’ epi prōton Nēlēïon elthemen andrōn,
ei tina hoi syn mētin amymona tektēnaito,
hē tis alexikakos pasin Danaoisi genoito.
sentences.l:
And this seemed to him in his heart the best plan,
to go to Nestor first, the Neleian, of men,
if with him some blameless cunning he might frame,
which might be evil-warding for all the Danaans.
sentences.i: And this seemed to him in his heart the best plan: to go first of all men to Nestor, son of Neleus, in case he might frame with him some blameless cunning that would ward off evil from all the Danaans.
sentences.n: ἥδε ‘this’ points forward to the infinitive clause in line 18, which is the plan itself. κατὰ θυμόν ‘in his heart’; ἀρίστη ‘best’; βουλή ‘plan’. ἐλθέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἐλθεῖν); Νηλήϊον is an adjective ‘of Neleus’ used like a patronymic, and πρῶτον … ἀνδρῶν ‘first of men’ means ahead of any other man. εἴ with the optative τεκτήναιτο ‘in case he might frame’ (the subject is Nestor); τεκταίνομαι is a carpenter’s verb, ‘build’, used of devising, and σύν is separated from it (tmesis): ‘frame together with him’. μῆτιν ‘cunning’ (cunning intelligence, here turned to framing a remedy); ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’. ἥ τις is ἥτις ‘which’. ἀλεξίκακος ‘warding off evil’ is built from ἀλέξω ‘ward off’ and κακόν ‘evil’. Δαναοῖσι is the dative plural of Δαναοί.

sentences.t:
ὀρθωθεὶς δ’ ἔνδυνε περὶ στήθεσσι χιτῶνα,
ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἔπειτα δαφοινὸν ἑέσσατο δέρμα λέοντος
αἴθωνος μεγάλοιο ποδηνεκές, εἵλετο δ’ ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
orthōtheis d’ endyne peri stēthessi chitōna,
possi d’ hypo liparoisin edēsato kala pedila,
amphi d’ epeita daphoinon heessato derma leontos
aithōnos megaloio podēnekes, heileto d’ enchos.
sentences.l:
Having raised himself upright, he put on about his chest the tunic,
and under his sleek feet he bound fine sandals,
and about him then the deep-red skin of a lion he put on,
tawny, great, reaching to the feet, and he took a spear.
sentences.i: He raised himself upright, put the tunic on over his chest, bound fine sandals beneath his sleek feet, and then put on the deep-red skin of a great tawny lion, reaching to his feet, and took a spear.
sentences.n: The arming goes by stages, each named by its own verb. ὀρθωθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὀρθόω ‘set upright’, ‘having raised himself’. ἔνδυνε ‘put on’ is an unaugmented imperfect; περί … στήθεσσι ‘about his chest’. Line 22 is word for word the line that also stands at 2.44. ἀμφὶ … ἑέσσατο is tmesis of ἀμφιέννυμι, with the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe oneself in’. δαφοινόν ‘deep-red’ has the intensive prefix δα- and φοινός ‘red’. αἴθωνος and μεγάλοιο are genitives with λέοντος ‘of a lion’; αἴθων is ‘burning’, and of a lion’s coat ‘tawny’. ποδηνεκές ‘reaching to the feet’ agrees with δέρμα. ἔγχος is ‘spear’.

sentences.t: ὣς δ’ αὔτως Μενέλαον ἔχε τρόμος·
sentences.tr: hōs d’ autōs Menelaon eche tromos·
sentences.l: So in the same way a trembling held Menelaus;
sentences.i: In the same way a trembling took hold of Menelaus;
sentences.n: With ὣς δ’ αὔτως ‘and in the same way’ the poem passes from Agamemnon to his brother, whose night is the same. ἔχε is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘held’; τρόμος ‘trembling’ is the subject, after the verb. The raised dot (·) stands in the middle of the line, so the unit ends there and the rest of the line begins the next one.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτῷ
ὕπνος ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἐφίζανε·
sentences.tr:
oude gar autōi
hypnos epi blepharoisin ephizane·
sentences.l:
for not even to him
sleep upon his eyelids settled;
sentences.i: for sleep did not settle on his eyelids either;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ γάρ gives the reason for the trembling: ‘for not even…’. αὐτῷ is ‘he himself’, here ‘he too’. ἐφίζανε is the imperfect of ἐφιζάνω ‘settle upon’; βλεφάροισιν is the epic dative plural of βλέφαρον ‘eyelid’. The same verb ἱζάνω comes back in Agamemnon’s mouth at line 92.

sentences.t:
μή τι πάθοιεν
Ἀργεῖοι, τοὶ δὴ ἕθεν εἵνεκα πουλὺν ἐφ’ ὑγρὴν
ἤλυθον ἐς Τροίην πόλεμον θρασὺν ὁρμαίνοντες.
sentences.tr:
mē ti pathoien
Argeioi, toi dē hethen heineka poulyn eph’ hygrēn
ēlython es Troiēn polemon thrasyn hormainontes.
sentences.l:
lest they suffer something,
the Argives, who indeed for his sake over the broad wet
came to Troy, pondering bold war.
sentences.i: lest the Argives come to harm, they who for his sake had crossed the wide sea to Troy, pondering bold war.
sentences.n: μή with the optative πάθοιεν (aorist of πάσχω) states a fear, and the verb of fearing is left unsaid: ‘[he was afraid] lest they suffer’; τι is ‘anything’, and so ‘harm’. τοὶ δή: the article is a relative, ‘who indeed’. ἕθεν is the epic genitive of the third-person pronoun, ‘him’, and ἕθεν εἵνεκα is ‘for his sake’. πουλύν is the epic form of πολύν; it is a masculine form beside the feminine ὑγρήν, and the construction is not quite clear. ὑγρήν ‘wet’ has its noun unsaid, and the sea is understood (compare ὑγρὰ κέλευθα ‘the watery ways’). ἤλυθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. ὁρμαίνοντες ‘pondering’ is the same participle as in line 4, here of men who came with war in their minds; θρασύν ‘bold’.

sentences.t:
παρδαλέῃ μὲν πρῶτα μετάφρενον εὐρὺ κάλυψε
ποικίλῃ, αὐτὰρ ἐπὶ στεφάνην κεφαλῆφιν ἀείρας
θήκατο χαλκείην, δόρυ δ’ εἵλετο χειρὶ παχείῃ.
sentences.tr:
pardaleēi men prōta metaphrenon eury kalypse
poikilēi, autar epi stephanēn kephalēphin aeiras
thēkato chalkeiēn, dory d’ heileto cheiri pacheiēi.
sentences.l:
With a leopard-skin, first, his broad back he covered,
dappled, and then upon his head, a circlet having lifted,
he set it on, a bronze one, and a spear he took in his stout hand.
sentences.i: First he covered his broad back with a dappled leopard-skin; then he lifted a bronze helmet onto his head and set it on, and took a spear in his stout hand.
sentences.n: παρδαλέῃ and ποικίλῃ are two feminine adjectives forming a noun phrase, ‘a dappled leopard-skin’, the dative of what covered him; μετάφρενον is the back, and κάλυψε is ‘covered’. πρῶτα ‘first’ begins the order of arming. στεφάνη is a word for something that goes round the head, from στέφω ‘put round’; here it is a helmet, but whether the word names the whole helmet or its rim is not certain, so the literal layer says ‘circlet’. κεφαλῆφιν has the suffix -φιν ‘on’; ἀείρας is the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’, and ἐπὶ … θήκατο is tmesis, ‘set on’ (θήκατο is the aorist middle of τίθημι). χαλκείην ‘of bronze’. δόρυ is ‘spear’, and χειρὶ παχείῃ ‘stout hand’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἀνστήσων ὃν ἀδελφεόν, ὃς μέγα πάντων
Ἀργείων ἤνασσε, θεὸς δ’ ὣς τίετο δήμῳ.
sentences.tr:
bē d’ imen anstēsōn hon adelpheon, hos mega pantōn
Argeiōn ēnasse, theos d’ hōs tieto dēmōi.
sentences.l:
And he went to go and rouse his own brother, who greatly over all
the Argives was lord, and like a god was honoured in the land.
sentences.i: He set out to rouse his brother, who was a great lord over all the Argives and was honoured in the land like a god.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν: βῆ is the aorist ‘went’ and ἴμεν the epic infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’; together they say that he set out. ἀνστήσων is the future participle of ἀνίστημι, ‘to rouse’, expressing purpose. ὃν ἀδελφεόν is ‘his own brother’ (ἀδελφεός is the epic ἀδελφός). The relative clause is about Agamemnon: ὃς μέγα πάντων Ἀργείων ἤνασσε, ‘who ruled greatly over all the Argives’, with ἀνάσσω taking the genitive. θεὸς δ’ ὣς is ‘and like a god’ (θεὸς ὥς); τίετο is the imperfect passive of τίω ‘honour’, and δήμῳ ‘in the land’ gives the place, with the people of the land in it.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ εὗρ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι τιθήμενον ἔντεα καλὰ
νηῒ πάρα πρύμνῃ·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ heur’ amph’ ōmoisi tithēmenon entea kala
nēï para prymnēi·
sentences.l:
Him he found putting about his shoulders his fine gear
beside the ship, at the stern;
sentences.i: He found him putting his fine gear about his shoulders, beside the stern of his ship;
sentences.n: τὸν is Agamemnon, the brother just named. εὗρ’ is εὗρε, ‘found’. τιθήμενον is the epic participle of the middle of τίθημι (= τιθέμενον), ‘putting on himself’, and ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι ‘about his shoulders’ goes with it. ἔντεα ‘gear’ is the arms; καλά ‘fine’. νηῒ πάρα πρύμνῃ is ‘beside the stern of the ship’ (πάρα = παρά, accented on the first syllable when it follows its noun; νηῒ is the epic dative of ναῦς). The raised dot ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἀσπάσιος γένετ’ ἐλθών.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ aspasios genet’ elthōn.
sentences.l: and to him a welcome sight he became, having come.
sentences.i: and he was a welcome sight to him as he came.
sentences.n: τῷ is the article as a pronoun, ‘to him’, Agamemnon; the subject is Menelaus, who has come. ἀσπάσιος is ‘welcome’ (a welcome sight), and γένετ’ is the unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι (= ἐγένετο); ἐλθών ‘having come, on coming’.

sentences.t: τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: ton proteros proseeipe boēn agathos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Him first addressed Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Menelaus, good at the war-cry, was the first to speak to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ … προσέειπε: the speech-introduction ‘addressed’, which the poem keeps apart from ἠμείβετο ‘answered’. πρότερος ‘first, before the other’ is an adjective where English uses an adverb. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the stock epithet of Menelaus (βοήν is an accusative of respect), translated every time. The edition prints no quotation marks, and the speech begins in the next line.

sentences.t: τίφθ’ οὕτως ἠθεῖε κορύσσεαι;
sentences.tr: tiphth’ houtōs ētheie korysseai;
sentences.l: “Why in this way, honoured one, are you arming?
sentences.i: “Why are you arming like this, my honoured one?
sentences.n: τίφθ’ is τίπτε (τί ποτε), an emphatic ‘why ever?’; οὕτως ‘in this way’. ἠθεῖε is a vocative of address, from ἠθεῖος, whose sense is not known: ‘honoured’ is the traditional guess. κορύσσεαι is the uncontracted second person of the middle of κορύσσω ‘arm’ (from κόρυς ‘helmet’; Attic κορύσσῃ). The question is asked on seeing a man armed at night.

sentences.t:
ἦ τιν’ ἑταίρων
ὀτρυνέεις Τρώεσσιν ἐπίσκοπον;
sentences.tr:
ē tin’ hetairōn
otryneeis Trōessin episkopon;
sentences.l:
Is it one of your companions
you will urge as a scout upon the Trojans?
sentences.i: Is it one of your companions you will urge to go as a scout on the Trojans?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question, ‘can it be that…?’. τιν’ is τινά ‘any’, with the partitive genitive ἑταίρων ‘of your companions’. ὀτρυνέεις is the uncontracted future of ὀτρύνω ‘urge’. ἐπίσκοπον ‘scout’ is a man sent to look, and Τρώεσσιν, the epic dative plural, says whom he is to look upon.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ αἰνῶς
δείδω μὴ οὔ τίς τοι ὑπόσχηται τόδε ἔργον
ἄνδρας δυσμενέας σκοπιαζέμεν οἶος ἐπελθὼν
νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην·
sentences.tr:
alla mal’ ainōs
deidō mē ou tis toi hyposchētai tode ergon
andras dysmeneas skopiazemen oios epelthōn
nykta di’ ambrosiēn·
sentences.l:
But very dreadfully
I fear lest no one for you undertake this task,
ill-disposed men to spy out, alone going against them
through the ambrosial night;
sentences.i: I am dreadfully afraid that no one will take this task on for you, going out alone against the ill-disposed men to spy on them through the ambrosial night;
sentences.n: ἀλλά here is ‘no, I fear…’, as an answer to his own question. μάλ’ αἰνῶς ‘very dreadfully’ goes with δείδω ‘I fear’. μὴ οὔ with the aorist subjunctive ὑπόσχηται (middle of ὑπέχω) states a fear that something will not happen, ‘lest no one undertake’; τοι is ‘for you’, and τόδε ἔργον ‘this task’. σκοπιαζέμεν is the epic infinitive of σκοπιάζω ‘spy out’, from σκοπιά ‘lookout’, and δυσμενέας ‘ill-disposed’ is the word for men set against you, here the Trojans. οἶος ‘alone’ agrees with the unnamed volunteer, and ἐπελθών is ‘having gone against’. νύκτα δι’ ἀμβροσίην is ‘through the ambrosial night’, the noun first and its adjective after the preposition.

sentences.t: μάλα τις θρασυκάρδιος ἔσται.
sentences.tr: mala tis thrasykardios estai.
sentences.l: very bold-hearted will someone be.”
sentences.i: it will take a very bold-hearted man.”
sentences.n: The sentence closes with a plain statement of what the task needs. τις ἔσται, ‘someone will be’, is a plain future: whoever goes will have to be very bold. θρασυκάρδιος ‘bold-hearted’ is built from θρασύς ‘bold’ and καρδία (the same word as κραδίη, ‘heart’).

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē kreiōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: In answer lord Agamemnon said to him:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ with προσέφη ‘addressed’. κρείων ‘lord’ is the epithet of Agamemnon in this formula, and it is kept apart from ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’.

sentences.t:
χρεὼ βουλῆς ἐμὲ καὶ σὲ διοτρεφὲς ὦ Μενέλαε
κερδαλέης, ἥ τίς κεν ἐρύσσεται ἠδὲ σαώσει
Ἀργείους καὶ νῆας, ἐπεὶ Διὸς ἐτράπετο φρήν.
sentences.tr:
chreō boulēs eme kai se diotrephes ō Menelae
kerdaleēs, hē tis ken eryssetai ēde saōsei
Argeious kai nēas, epei Dios etrapeto phrēn.
sentences.l:
“Need of a plan is upon me and you, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus,
a shrewd one, such as may protect and save
the Argives and the ships, since of Zeus the mind has turned.
sentences.i: “There is need of a plan, for you and for me, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, a shrewd plan that may protect and save the Argives and the ships, since the mind of Zeus has turned.
sentences.n: χρεώ ‘need’ has no verb and takes a genitive of the thing needed, βουλῆς ‘of a plan’, and an accusative of the persons, ἐμὲ καὶ σέ. διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured’ is the stock epithet of kings, in the vocative, and ὦ Μενέλαε follows it. κερδαλέης ‘shrewd’ (from κέρδος ‘gain, advantage’) agrees with βουλῆς. ἥ τις is ἥτις ‘one which’; ἐρύσσεται (from ἐρύομαι ‘protect’) and σαώσει (σαόω ‘save’) go with κεν, ‘such as may protect and save’. ἐτράπετο is the aorist middle of τρέπω ‘turn’: the mind of Zeus has turned away, and the next line says where to.

sentences.t: Ἑκτορέοις ἄρα μᾶλλον ἐπὶ φρένα θῆχ’ ἱεροῖσιν·
sentences.tr: Hektoreois ara mallon epi phrena thēch’ hieroisin·
sentences.l: To Hector’s sacrifices, it seems, rather his mind he has set;
sentences.i: It is rather on Hector’s sacrifices, it seems, that he has set his mind;
sentences.n: Ἑκτορέοις is an adjective ‘of Hector’ agreeing with ἱεροῖσιν; ἱερά in the plural is ‘sacrifices’, the offerings made to Zeus. ἐπὶ … θῆχ’ is tmesis of ἐπιτίθημι: θῆχ’ is θῆκε, elided, ‘set upon’, and φρένα is the object, ‘his mind’ (the singular, where line 10 had the plural). ἄρα ‘then, it seems’ marks a conclusion newly drawn; μᾶλλον is ‘rather’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω ἰδόμην, οὐδ’ ἔκλυον αὐδήσαντος
ἄνδρ’ ἕνα τοσσάδε μέρμερ’ ἐπ’ ἤματι μητίσασθαι,
ὅσσ’ Ἕκτωρ ἔρρεξε Διῒ φίλος υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
αὔτως, οὔτε θεᾶς υἱὸς φίλος οὔτε θεοῖο.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō idomēn, oud’ eklyon audēsantos
andr’ hena tossade mermer’ ep’ ēmati mētisasthai,
hoss’ Hektōr errexe Diï philos huias Achaiōn
autōs, oute theas huios philos oute theoio.
sentences.l:
For never yet have I seen, nor heard from one who told it,
a single man devise so many baneful things in one day
as Hector, dear to Zeus, did to the sons of the Achaeans,
just so, being neither the dear son of a goddess nor of a god.
sentences.i: For I have never yet seen, nor heard anyone tell of it, a single man devising in one day so many baneful things as Hector, dear to Zeus, has done to the sons of the Achaeans, and all as a mere man, neither the dear son of a goddess nor of a god.
sentences.n: γάρ backs the claim of line 46 with what Hector has done. ἰδόμην is the epic aorist middle of ὁράω (= εἶδον), and ἔκλυον ‘heard’ takes the genitive of the speaker, αὐδήσαντος ‘one who said it’. Both govern the infinitive μητίσασθαι ‘to devise’ (aorist middle of μητίομαι) with ἄνδρ’ ἕνα ‘one man’ as subject. τοσσάδε … ὅσσ’ is ‘so many … as’; μέρμερα ‘baneful things’ is a word of uncertain origin. ἔρρεξε is the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do’, with the doubled ρ; Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’; υἷας is the accusative plural of υἱός. αὔτως here is ‘just so, merely’, and the last line says what Hector is not: not the dear son of a goddess or of a god, a mere mortal.

sentences.t:
ἔργα δ’ ἔρεξ’ ὅσα φημὶ μελησέμεν Ἀργείοισι
δηθά τε καὶ δολιχόν· τόσα γὰρ κακὰ μήσατ’ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
erga d’ erex’ hosa phēmi melēsemen Argeioisi
dētha te kai dolichon· tosa gar kaka mēsat’ Achaious.
sentences.l:
And deeds he has done such as, I say, will be a care to the Argives
long and for long; so many evils has he devised against the Achaeans.
sentences.i: He has done deeds that, I say, will be a care to the Argives for a long, long time; so many evils has he devised against the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἔργα δ’ ἔρεξ’ takes up the verb of line 49, with Hector still the subject. ὅσα ‘of such a kind as’, and φημί ‘I say’ takes the future infinitive μελησέμεν (epic -έμεν for -ειν) of μέλω ‘be a care’: the deeds will weigh on the Argives. δηθά ‘for a long time’ and δολιχόν (the neuter of δολιχός ‘long’ used as an adverb) are a pair, ‘long and for long’. μήσατ’ is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise’, with Ἀχαιούς ‘against the Achaeans’. The poet uses Argives and Achaeans in two lines for the same army.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν Αἴαντα καὶ Ἰδομενῆα κάλεσσον
ῥίμφα θέων παρὰ νῆας·
sentences.tr:
all’ ithi nyn Aianta kai Idomenēa kalesson
rhimpha theōn para nēas·
sentences.l:
But go now, Ajax and Idomeneus call,
running nimbly along the ships;
sentences.i: But go now and call Ajax and Idomeneus, running nimbly along the ships;
sentences.n: ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’ and κάλεσσον the aorist imperative of καλέω ‘call’ (the doubled σ is for the metre). Αἴαντα is a singular, one Ajax, and the line does not say which. Ἰδομενῆα is the accusative of Ἰδομενεύς. ῥίμφα ‘nimbly’ goes with θέων, the participle of θέω ‘run’; παρὰ νῆας ‘along the ships’.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐπὶ Νέστορα δῖον
εἶμι, καὶ ὀτρυνέω ἀνστήμεναι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν
ἐλθεῖν ἐς φυλάκων ἱερὸν τέλος ἠδ’ ἐπιτεῖλαι.
sentences.tr:
egō d’ epi Nestora dion
eimi, kai otryneō anstēmenai, ai k’ ethelēisin
elthein es phylakōn hieron telos ēd’ epiteilai.
sentences.l:
and I to heavenly Nestor
will go, and I will urge him to rise, if perhaps he is willing
to come to the sacred company of the guards and to give charge.
sentences.i: I myself will go to heavenly Nestor and urge him to rise, in case he is willing to come to the sacred company of the guards and give them their charge.
sentences.n: ἐγὼ δ’ sets Agamemnon’s own errand against the one he gave. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet. εἶμι ‘I will go’ is a present with future sense; ὀτρυνέω is the uncontracted future of ὀτρύνω ‘urge’, and ἀνστήμεναι the epic aorist infinitive of ἀνίστημι, here intransitive, ‘to stand up’. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν is ‘if perhaps he is willing’ (αἴ κε = εἰ with the subjunctive). ἐλθεῖν and ἐπιτεῖλαι (aorist infinitive of ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, give a charge’) depend on it. φυλάκων is the genitive plural of φύλαξ ‘guard’, and τέλος here is ‘company’, a body of men, with ἱερόν ‘sacred’ as its epithet.

sentences.t: κείνῳ γάρ κε μάλιστα πιθοίατο·
sentences.tr: keinōi gar ke malista pithoiato·
sentences.l: For him most of all would they obey;
sentences.i: He is the one they would obey above all others;
sentences.n: κείνῳ is the epic form of ἐκείνῳ ‘that man’, Nestor, in the dative with πιθοίατο, an optative of πείθομαι ‘obey’ (-οίατο is the old third plural ending). κε makes it conditional, ‘they would’. γάρ explains why Nestor, not another.

sentences.t:
τοῖο γὰρ υἱὸς
σημαίνει φυλάκεσσι καὶ Ἰδομενῆος ὀπάων
Μηριόνης·
sentences.tr:
toio gar huios
sēmainei phylakessi kai Idomenēos opaōn
Mērionēs·
sentences.i: for his son gives orders to the guards, and so does Meriones, the follower of Idomeneus;
sentences.n: τοῖο is the epic genitive of the article as pronoun, ‘of him’, and τοῖο … υἱός is ‘his son’, who is not named. σημαίνει is ‘gives a sign’, and so ‘gives orders’; the singular verb stands for both subjects, the son and Μηριόνης. ὀπάων ‘follower’ is the one who goes with a chief, here Idomeneus’. φυλάκεσσι is the epic dative plural of φύλαξ.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν γὰρ ἐπετράπομέν γε μάλιστα.
sentences.tr: toisin gar epetrapomen ge malista.
sentences.l: for to them we entrusted it most of all.”
sentences.i: for it is to these two above all that we entrusted the watch.”
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘to them’, the two men just named. ἐπετράπομεν is the aorist of ἐπιτρέπω, here ‘entrust, hand over’, with its object, the watch, left unsaid; it is a different sense of the verb from ‘yield’ at line 79. γε is ‘at least, indeed’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita boēn agathos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Him then answered Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Then Menelaus, good at the war-cry, answered him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula with ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, kept apart from ‘addressed’ (προσέειπε). Menelaus’ epithet βοὴν ἀγαθός is translated again, as in line 36.

sentences.t: πῶς γάρ μοι μύθῳ ἐπιτέλλεαι ἠδὲ κελεύεις;
sentences.tr: pōs gar moi mythōi epitelleai ēde keleueis;
sentences.l: “How, then, to me in word do you enjoin and command?
sentences.i: “How, then, do you charge and command me with your words?
sentences.n: γάρ in a question ties it to what has just been said, ‘how, then…?’. ἐπιτέλλεαι is the uncontracted second person of the middle of ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, give a charge’; κελεύεις ‘you command’; μύθῳ ‘in word’. The two questions that follow say what Menelaus cannot tell: whether he is to wait or to follow.

sentences.t:
αὖθι μένω μετὰ τοῖσι δεδεγμένος εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθῃς,
ἦε θέω μετὰ σ’ αὖτις, ἐπὴν εὖ τοῖς ἐπιτείλω;
sentences.tr:
authi menō meta toisi dedegmenos eis ho ken elthēis,
ēe theō meta s’ autis, epēn eu tois epiteilō;
sentences.l:
Am I to stay here among them, waiting until you come,
or to run after you again, when I have given them good charge?”
sentences.i: Am I to stay here with them and wait until you come, or run after you again, once I have charged them properly?”
sentences.n: μένω and θέω are subjunctives of deliberation (the short-vowel form), ‘am I to stay…, or am I to run…?’, joined by ἦε ‘or’. αὖθι ‘here, on the spot’. μετὰ τοῖσι ‘among them’ means the men he is to call. δεδεγμένος is the perfect participle of δέχομαι, ‘waiting’, and εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθῃς is ‘until you come’. μετὰ σ’ with the accusative is ‘after you’. ἐπήν ‘when’ takes the aorist subjunctive ἐπιτείλω ‘I have given charge’, as at line 56; εὖ is ‘well’, and τοῖς ‘to them’ is the article as pronoun.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων,
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen anax andrōn Agamemnōn,
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is the formula that stands elsewhere with a raised dot at its end; here the edition prints a comma, and the speech opens with an infinitive. The unit stops at the comma all the same, so that the speech can begin a unit of its own. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the epithet of Agamemnon, and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the second speaker answering the first.

sentences.t:
αὖθι μένειν, μή πως ἀβροτάξομεν ἀλλήλοιιν
ἐρχομένω·
sentences.tr:
authi menein, mē pōs abrotaxomen allēloiin
erchomenō·
sentences.l:
“Stay here, lest somehow we miss each other,
the two of us going;
sentences.i: “Stay here, in case we somehow miss each other as we go;
sentences.n: αὖθι μένειν is an infinitive standing for an imperative, ‘stay here’, and answers Menelaus’ first question. μή πως with the subjunctive ἀβροτάξομεν is ‘lest somehow we miss’: the verb, built on the root of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’, is rare. ἀλλήλοιιν ‘each other’ and ἐρχομένω ‘going’ are duals, the Greek number for a pair, here the two brothers.

sentences.t: πολλαὶ γὰρ ἀνὰ στρατόν εἰσι κέλευθοι.
sentences.tr: pollai gar ana straton eisi keleuthoi.
sentences.l: for many are the ways up through the army.
sentences.i: for there are many ways through the army.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for staying put. κέλευθοι ‘ways’ is the plural of κέλευθος; ἀνὰ στρατόν ‘up through the army’.

sentences.t:
φθέγγεο δ’ ᾗ κεν ἴῃσθα καὶ ἐγρήγορθαι ἄνωχθι
πατρόθεν ἐκ γενεῆς ὀνομάζων ἄνδρα ἕκαστον
πάντας κυδαίνων·
sentences.tr:
phthengeo d’ hēi ken iēistha kai egrēgorthai anōchthi
patrothen ek geneēs onomazōn andra hekaston
pantas kydainōn·
sentences.i: Call out wherever you go, and tell them to stay awake, naming each man by his father’s name and his lineage and giving glory to them all;
sentences.n: φθέγγεο is the uncontracted imperative (= φθέγγου) of φθέγγομαι ‘call out, make your voice heard’. ᾗ κεν ἴῃσθα is ‘wherever you may go’ (a subjunctive of εἶμι with the ending -ῃσθα). ἐγρήγορθαι is the perfect infinitive of ἐγείρω, ‘to be awake’, and ἄνωχθι the imperative of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, which takes it; the persons bidden are left to the sense. πατρόθεν ‘from the father’ is naming a man by his father, and ἐκ γενεῆς ‘from his lineage’ adds the family; ὀνομάζων ‘naming’, with ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ‘each man’. κυδαίνων ‘giving glory to’ (from κῦδος ‘glory’) is to treat each man as one worth honour.

sentences.t:
μηδὲ μεγαλίζεο θυμῷ,
ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοί περ πονεώμεθα·
sentences.tr:
mēde megalizeo thymōi,
alla kai autoi per poneōmetha·
sentences.l:
and do not be lofty in spirit,
but let us ourselves too toil;
sentences.i: and do not carry yourself loftily in spirit, but let us labour ourselves as well;
sentences.n: μεγαλίζεο is the uncontracted imperative of μεγαλίζομαι ‘think oneself great, be lofty’; μηδέ ‘and not’; θυμῷ ‘in spirit’. Menelaus must not stand on his rank when he calls the others. πονεώμεθα is a subjunctive of exhortation, ‘let us toil’, from πονέομαι, with the open vowels the epic allows. καὶ αὐτοί περ is ‘ourselves too, in our own persons’.

sentences.t:
ὧδέ που ἄμμι
Ζεὺς ἐπὶ γιγνομένοισιν ἵει κακότητα βαρεῖαν.
sentences.tr:
hōde pou ammi
Zeus epi gignomenoisin hiei kakotēta bareian.
sentences.l:
so, I suppose, to us
Zeus, as we were being born, sent evil, heavy.”
sentences.i: That, I suppose, is how Zeus laid heavy misfortune on us from the hour of our birth.”
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘thus’, and που ‘I suppose’, soften a bitter reflection. ἄμμι is the Aeolic dative of ἡμεῖς ‘to us’. ἐπὶ γιγνομένοισιν is a dative plural participle, ‘upon us as we were being born’. ἵει is the unaugmented imperfect of ἵημι ‘send, let go’; κακότητα is ‘misfortune, evil lot’, and βαρεῖαν ‘heavy’. The point is that hardship has been their lot since birth, so neither of them should hold back from the work.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἀπέπεμπεν ἀδελφεὸν εὖ ἐπιτείλας·
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn apepempen adelpheon eu epiteilas·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he sent his brother away, well having given charge;
sentences.i: With these words he sent his brother off, having charged him well;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes the speech. ἀπέπεμπεν is the imperfect of ἀποπέμπω ‘send off’; ἀδελφεόν ‘brother’; ἐπιτείλας is the aorist participle of ἐπιτέλλω ‘give a charge’, with εὖ ‘well’, matching the charge Menelaus asked about in line 63.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ ῥ’ ἰέναι μετὰ Νέστορα ποιμένα λαῶν·
sentences.tr: autar ho bē rh’ ienai meta Nestora poimena laōn·
sentences.l: but he set out to go after Nestor, shepherd of the people;
sentences.i: and he for his part set out to find Nestor, shepherd of the people;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ: ὅ, the article as pronoun, is Agamemnon, who now goes his own way while his brother goes to the others. βῆ ῥ’ ἰέναι is ‘set out to go’ (ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle); μετά with the accusative is ‘in quest of’. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the title given to Agamemnon in line 3, here given to Nestor.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ εὗρεν παρά τε κλισίῃ καὶ νηῒ μελαίνῃ
εὐνῇ ἔνι μαλακῇ·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ heuren para te klisiēi kai nēï melainēi
eunēi eni malakēi·
sentences.l:
Him he found beside his hut and black ship
in a soft couch;
sentences.i: He found him by his hut and his black ship, on a soft couch;
sentences.n: τὸν is Nestor. εὗρεν ‘found’; παρά τε … καὶ ‘beside both … and’. κλισίῃ ‘hut’ is the shelter of a chief, and νηῒ μελαίνῃ ‘black ship’ is the stock phrase for a ship drawn up on the shore. ἔνι is ἐν, placed between noun and adjective: εὐνῇ ἔνι μαλακῇ ‘in a soft couch’. The raised dot ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t:
παρὰ δ’ ἔντεα ποικίλ’ ἔκειτο
ἀσπὶς καὶ δύο δοῦρε φαεινή τε τρυφάλεια.
sentences.tr:
para d’ entea poikil’ ekeito
aspis kai dyo doure phaeinē te tryphaleia.
sentences.l:
and beside lay inlaid gear,
a shield and two spears and a shining helm.
sentences.i: Beside him lay his inlaid gear: a shield, two spears and a shining helmet.
sentences.n: παρά here is an adverb, ‘beside’. ἔκειτο is the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, a singular verb with the neuter plural ἔντεα ‘gear’; ποικίλ’ (ποικίλα) ‘inlaid’ is the word for worked metal with a pattern. ἀσπίς, δοῦρε and τρυφάλεια stand in apposition, naming the pieces. δοῦρε is the dual of δόρυ ‘spear’, matching δύο ‘two’. φαεινή ‘shining’ is a stock epithet; τρυφάλεια ‘helm’ is a word of unknown origin.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δὲ ζωστὴρ κεῖτο παναίολος, ᾧ ῥ’ ὁ γεραιὸς
ζώννυθ’ ὅτ’ ἐς πόλεμον φθισήνορα θωρήσσοιτο
λαὸν ἄγων, ἐπεὶ οὐ μὲν ἐπέτρεπε γήραϊ λυγρῷ.
sentences.tr:
par de zōstēr keito panaiolos, hōi rh’ ho geraios
zōnnyth’ hot’ es polemon phthisēnora thōrēssoito
laon agōn, epei ou men epetrepe gēraï lygrōi.
sentences.l:
and beside lay a belt, all-glancing, with which the old man
girt himself whenever for man-wasting war he armed himself,
leading the people, since he did not yield to grievous old age.
sentences.i: Beside it lay a belt, all-glancing, which the old man would gird on whenever he armed himself for the war that wastes men and led his troops, for he would not give way to grievous old age.
sentences.n: πὰρ δέ is παρὰ δέ with the vowel cut off: a second thing laid beside him, the belt. κεῖτο ‘lay’. ζωστήρ is a belt; παναίολος is ‘all-glancing’ (παν- ‘all’ and αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’), and whether it gleams or is many-coloured is not certain. ᾧ is a dative relative, ‘with which’; ὁ γεραιός ‘the old man’ is Nestor. ζώννυθ’ is the unaugmented imperfect middle of ζώννυμι ‘gird’, and with ὅτε and the optative θωρήσσοιτο (θωρήσσομαι ‘arm oneself’) it describes a habit. φθισήνορα ‘man-wasting’ is from φθίω ‘waste’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’. λαὸν ἄγων ‘leading the people’. ἐπέτρεπε is the imperfect of ἐπιτρέπω, here ‘yield, give way’ with the dative; λυγρῷ ‘grievous’. γήραϊ is the dative of γῆρας ‘old age’.

sentences.t:
ὀρθωθεὶς δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ ἀγκῶνος κεφαλὴν ἐπαείρας
Ἀτρεΐδην προσέειπε καὶ ἐξερεείνετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr:
orthōtheis d’ ar’ ep’ ankōnos kephalēn epaeiras
Atreïdēn proseeipe kai exereeineto mythōi·
sentences.l:
Having raised himself upright on an elbow, and lifted up his head,
he addressed Atreus’-son and questioned him in words:
sentences.i: Propping himself on his elbow and lifting his head, he spoke to the son of Atreus and questioned him:
sentences.n: ὀρθωθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὀρθόω, ‘having raised himself’, and ἐπ’ ἀγκῶνος ‘on an elbow’ is the genitive of what he leans on. ἐπαείρας is the aorist participle of ἐπαείρω ‘lift up’, with κεφαλήν as its object. Ἀτρεΐδην ‘son of Atreus’ is the poet’s name for Agamemnon, whom Nestor does not yet know. προσέειπε ‘addressed’ and ἐξερεείνετο, the imperfect middle of ἐξερεείνω ‘question closely’, are joined by καί; μύθῳ is ‘in words’.

sentences.l:
“And who are you, this one, who along the ships, up through the army, come alone
through the murky night, when other mortals sleep,
either seeking one of the mules, or one of your companions?
sentences.i: “Who are you, going alone among the ships and through the army in the murky night, when other mortals sleep, in search of one of the mules or of one of your companions?
sentences.n: τίς δ’ οὗτος, ‘and who is this?’, is joined to a verb of the second person, ἔρχεαι (the uncontracted form of ἔρχῃ), so the sense is ‘who are you who come…?’. Nestor cannot see him. κατὰ νῆας ‘along the ships’, ἀνὰ στρατόν ‘up through the army’, and οἶος ‘alone’. νύκτα δι’ ὀρφναίην is ‘through the murky night’; ὅτε θ’ εὕδουσι ‘when they sleep’ (the τε marks it as a general fact). οὐρήων is the epic genitive plural of οὐρεύς ‘mule’, and τιν’ οὐρήων is ‘one of the mules’; διζήμενος ‘seeking’ is the participle of δίζημαι. ἠέ … ἤ is ‘either … or’.

sentences.t: φθέγγεο, μηδ’ ἀκέων ἐπ’ ἔμ’ ἔρχεο·
sentences.tr: phthengeo, mēd’ akeōn ep’ em’ ercheo·
sentences.l: Speak, and do not in silence come at me;
sentences.i: Speak, and do not come at me in silence;
sentences.n: φθέγγεο ‘speak out’ is the same imperative as at line 67. ἀκέων ‘in silence’ is an adjective agreeing with the subject, where English uses an adverb. ἐπ’ ἔμ’ ἔρχεο is ‘come upon me’ (ἔμ’ is ἐμέ, elided; ἔρχεο is the uncontracted imperative). A man who approaches a sleeper without a word is a threat, and Nestor says so.

sentences.t: τίπτε δέ σε χρεώ;
sentences.tr: tipte de se chreō;
sentences.l: and what need is upon you?”
sentences.i: What do you need?”
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε, ‘what ever?’. χρεώ ‘need’ has no verb here, and takes the accusative of the person, σε, as at line 43: ‘what need is upon you?’, that is, what has brought you.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then answered the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, answered him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula with ἠμείβετο ‘answered’ and Agamemnon’s epithet ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’.

sentences.t:
ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν
γνώσεαι Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα, τὸν περὶ πάντων
Ζεὺς ἐνέηκε πόνοισι διαμπερὲς εἰς ὅ κ’ ἀϋτμὴ
ἐν στήθεσσι μένῃ καί μοι φίλα γούνατ’ ὀρώρῃ.
sentences.tr:
ō Nestor Nēlēïadē mega kydos Achaiōn
gnōseai Atreïdēn Agamemnona, ton peri pantōn
Zeus eneēke ponoisi diamperes eis ho k’ aÿtmē
en stēthessi menēi kai moi phila gounat’ orōrēi.
sentences.l:
“O Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,
you will know Atreus’-son Agamemnon, whom above all
Zeus has put into toils continually, for as long as breath
in my chest remains and my dear knees are stirred.
sentences.i: “Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, you will know Agamemnon, son of Atreus, whom Zeus, beyond all others, has put into toils without ceasing, for as long as breath stays in my chest and my knees can move.
sentences.n: Line 87 is a full vocative address, the same words as in the Odyssey. Νηληϊάδη is the vocative of a patronymic, ‘son of Neleus’. γνώσεαι is the uncontracted future of γιγνώσκω ‘know, recognise’; Agamemnon answers ‘who are you?’ by naming himself in the third person. τὸν … ἐνέηκε: τόν is a relative, ‘whom’, περὶ πάντων is ‘above all’, and ἐνέηκε is the aorist of ἐνίημι ‘put into’, with πόνοισι ‘toils’ (the dative plural of πόνος). διαμπερές ‘without ceasing’. The words from εἰς ὅ κ’ to the end of line 90 are the same as at 9.609–610, where Zeus’ portion holds a man at the ships; here they turn to Agamemnon’s own labours. φίλα is ‘my own’, and ὀρώρῃ the perfect subjunctive of ὄρνυμι, ‘are stirred’.

sentences.t:
πλάζομαι ὧδ’ ἐπεὶ οὔ μοι ἐπ’ ὄμμασι νήδυμος ὕπνος
ἱζάνει, ἀλλὰ μέλει πόλεμος καὶ κήδε’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
plazomai hōd’ epei ou moi ep’ ommasi nēdymos hypnos
hizanei, alla melei polemos kai kēde’ Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
I wander thus, since not on my eyes sweet sleep
settles, but war is a care to me, and the sorrows of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: I wander about like this because sweet sleep does not settle on my eyes, but war and the sorrows of the Achaeans are my care.
sentences.n: πλάζομαι is the passive of πλάζω ‘drive astray’, so ‘I am driven about, I wander’; ὧδε ‘thus’; ἐπεί ‘since’. οὔ μοι … ἱζάνει is ‘does not settle for me’, the verb already used of Menelaus at line 26, and ὄμμασι the epic dative plural of ὄμμα ‘eye’. νήδυμος ὕπνος ‘sweet sleep’: the meaning of νήδυμος is not known, and ‘sweet’ is the traditional guess; it is a different word from the γλυκερός ‘sweet’ of line 4. μέλει ‘is a care’ has two subjects, πόλεμος and κήδεα ‘sorrows’, and the verb is the one used at line 51.

sentences.t:
αἰνῶς γὰρ Δαναῶν περιδείδια, οὐδέ μοι ἦτορ
ἔμπεδον, ἀλλ’ ἀλαλύκτημαι, κραδίη δέ μοι ἔξω
στηθέων ἐκθρῴσκει, τρομέει δ’ ὑπὸ φαίδιμα γυῖα.
sentences.tr:
ainōs gar Danaōn perideidia, oude moi ētor
empedon, all’ alalyktēmai, kradiē de moi exō
stētheōn ekthrōiskei, tromeei d’ hypo phaidima guia.
sentences.l:
For dreadfully for the Danaans I am afraid, and my heart is not
firm, but I am distraught, and my heart out of
my chest leaps, and beneath me tremble my glorious limbs.
sentences.i: I am dreadfully afraid for the Danaans, and my heart is not firm; I am distraught, and my heart leaps out of my chest, and my glorious limbs tremble beneath me.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for his wandering. αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’ goes with περιδείδια, a perfect of περιδείδω ‘fear greatly for’ whose sense is present, with the genitive Δαναῶν ‘for the Danaans’. οὐδέ μοι ἦτορ ἔμπεδον ‘nor is my heart firm’, the verb ‘is’ left out. ἀλαλύκτημαι is a perfect meaning ‘I am distraught, beside myself’; the verb is rare and its formation is not certain. ἔξω στηθέων ‘out of my chest’, with the genitive plural στηθέων of στῆθος; ἐκθρῴσκει ‘leaps out’. τρομέει is uncontracted (= τρομεῖ); ὑπό is an adverb, ‘beneath’. φαίδιμα ‘glorious’ is a stock epithet, here of the limbs (γυῖα). Heart and limbs shake as his wits did in line 10.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴ τι δραίνεις, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ σέ γ’ ὕπνος ἱκάνει,
δεῦρ’ ἐς τοὺς φύλακας καταβήομεν, ὄφρα ἴδωμεν
μὴ τοὶ μὲν καμάτῳ ἀδηκότες ἠδὲ καὶ ὕπνῳ
κοιμήσωνται, ἀτὰρ φυλακῆς ἐπὶ πάγχυ λάθωνται.
sentences.tr:
all’ ei ti draineis, epei oude se g’ hypnos hikanei,
deur’ es tous phylakas katabēomen, ophra idōmen
mē toi men kamatōi adēkotes ēde kai hypnōi
koimēsōntai, atar phylakēs epi panchy lathōntai.
sentences.l:
But if you are minded to do anything, since not even you does sleep come upon,
come here, let us go down to the guards, so that we may see,
lest they, worn out by weariness and also by sleep,
have lain down to sleep, and of the watch altogether forget.
sentences.i: But if you mean to do something, since sleep does not come to you either, come, let us go down to the guards, to see that they have not lain down to sleep, worn out by weariness and by sleep, and forgotten their watch altogether.
sentences.n: δραίνεις is from a rare verb taken to be related to δράω ‘do’; ‘be minded to do’ is the usual gloss. ἐπεί ‘since’, with οὐδὲ σέ γ’ ‘not even you’; ἱκάνει ‘comes to’. δεῦρο ‘come here’, an invitation, is followed by the subjunctive καταβήομεν (lengthened vowel; καταβαίνω ‘go down’), ‘let us go down’. ὄφρα ἴδωμεν is ‘so that we may see’; μή with κοιμήσωνται and λάθωνται gives the fear behind the looking, ‘(to see) that they have not…’. τοὶ μέν: the article is a pronoun, ‘they’. ἀδηκότες is the perfect participle of a verb meaning ‘be worn out’, whose sense is not quite certain; καμάτῳ ‘weariness’ and ὕπνῳ ‘sleep’ say by what. ἐπὶ … λάθωνται is tmesis of ἐπιλανθάνομαι ‘forget’, which takes the genitive φυλακῆς ‘watch’; πάγχυ ‘altogether’.

sentences.t: δυσμενέες δ’ ἄνδρες σχεδὸν εἵαται·
sentences.tr: dysmenees d’ andres schedon heiatai·
sentences.l: Ill-disposed men are seated near;
sentences.i: Ill-disposed men are camped close by;
sentences.n: δυσμενέες ‘ill-disposed’ are the Trojans; σχεδόν ‘near’. εἵαται is the epic third plural of ἧμαι ‘sit’, ‘they are seated’, and so, of an army, ‘encamped’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι ἴδμεν
μή πως καὶ διὰ νύκτα μενοινήσωσι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
oude ti idmen
mē pōs kai dia nykta menoinēsōsi machesthai.
sentences.l:
and not at all do we know
lest perhaps even through the night they may be minded to fight.”
sentences.i: and for all we know they may be minded to fight even in the night.”
sentences.n: ἴδμεν is the epic first plural of οἶδα (= ἴσμεν), ‘we know’; οὐδέ τι ‘and not at all’. μή πως with the subjunctive μενοινήσωσι makes the possibility a fear: ‘(we do not know) lest perhaps they…’. μενοινάω is ‘have in mind, be eager’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’; καὶ διὰ νύκτα is ‘even through the night’.
